Why the Book of Revelation Is About Hope, Not Fear: A Guide to Revelation 1–22

Michael Rowntree

|

October 9, 2026
Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 12:43
Instaread

Those who don’t obsess over Revelation tend to neglect it. In the words of Watchman Nee, “This book is a record filled with disasters, calamities, curses, troubles, and warnings. No wonder it is not accepted by man.”

If I had penned the book of Revelation, I would have bypassed monsters and demon armies. I would have raced straight to the heavenly city. My epistle would have been shorter than 3 John, and I would have given dates.

But “my thoughts are not your thoughts… declares the LORD” (Isa. 55:8, ESV throughout).

Nee explains why people resist Revelation. But more than he acknowledges, this book is a record filled with beauty, blessing, praise, joy, and hope.

These features are not just hidden nuggets, either. They are primary. The book of Revelation confronts us with scary images, but God’s goal is not to give his children nightmares. It’s to show us what we’re up against. Only then can we fully appreciate the One who fights for us — the One Satan is up against.

Hope in Revelation flows from the heart of our triune God (Rev. 1:4–5). It rushes over the cliff-edge of heaven and floods every chapter.

Let’s take a tour.

Why the Book of Revelation Begins with Jesus (Ch. 1)

Consider John’s opening phrase, “the revelation of Jesus Christ” (Rev. 1:1). That word, revelation, derives from the Greek word apokalypsis. In English, the related term, apocalypse, conjures images of zombies and nuclear bombs. According to scholars, however, the term means “unveiling.”

Revelation is a backstage pass for the unveiling of Jesus Christ.

The unveiling takes two forms: First, it is Jesus’ unveiling of the Father’s plan to make the world right; second, it is the unveiling of Jesus himself. Both inspire hope, but the latter surpasses the former.

This explains why one glimpse of Jesus struck John to the ground (1:17). You’d crater too if you saw what John saw. This wasn’t the lowly Jesus of the Gospels. It was the exalted “ruler of the kings of the earth” (1:5), whose “eyes were like a flame of fire” and “whose face was like the sun shining in full strength” (1:14, 16). If Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John reflect Christ in his humiliation, the book of Revelation presents him in splendor. How tragic that so many — out of fear and confusion — have discarded the book of Scripture most overtly dedicated to the exaltation of King Jesus.

The book of Revelation begins with Jesus for a reason. If you fear the Lord, you won’t fear the enemy.

You won’t fear tribulation. And you definitely won’t fear John’s visions.

Jesus Prepares His Church (Rev. 2–3)

Revelation 1 concludes with Jesus walking — not in the halls of Congress — but among seven golden lampstands: the seven churches. We are where he wants to be.

This becomes more remarkable when you consider the “we” of Revelation 2–3. Most of the seven churches are weak and struggling. Only two avoid a rebuke. Three are warned. Despite their sin, Immanuel refuses to keep distance. All seven churches receive personal attention.

“Seven” appears 54 times in the book of Revelation, and it represents completion. These were seven literal assemblies, but together they symbolize the “complete” church, from then until the end. Despite our sins, “the first and the last” makes church his first priority (2:8).

Our Great High Priest draws near to comfort us; however, he also readies us for what comes next. He trims our wick, supplies the oil, and keeps every lampstand burning. Revelation 2 and 3 appear where they do — before the darkest hours — to prepare us.

Jesus is the ultimate prepper.

The Father Who Sits, the Lamb Who Stands (Rev. 4–5)

Nowhere is God’s sovereign reign more dramatized than in this scene. The word “throne” appears 18 times in Revelation 4–5. Before we ever face the “monsters” that make Revelation famous, God reveals the command center of creation: his throne.

Heaven is alive with the sound of music, and the sights are equally majestic. John beholds a “sea of glass” (4:6). Lightning and thunder portend judgment — yet the sea underneath is tame. More precisely, it is tamed.

Throughout Scripture, the sea represents chaos and evil. But here before God’s throne, not one ripple of injustice can transgress its border.

This is one of Revelation’s great themes. Evil is terrifying but contained. Its power is granted (6:8; 13:5, 7), limited (9:4–5; 20:1–3), timed (2:10; 9:14–15; 11:2; 12:12), conditioned (11:7), frustrated (12:14), subordinated (17:17), and ultimately — crushed (20:7–10).

Chaos lies captive before our Father’s throne.

If Revelation 4 pictures evil contained, Revelation 5 shows evil conquered. Our Father holds a scroll, which reveals his plan for judging and redeeming the world.

Yet John sobs. He sobs “because no one was found worthy to open the scroll or to look into it” (5:4). Even a perfect plan requires the right Person to execute it.

Israel had long awaited the promised Lion of Judah and Davidic King who would conquer their oppressors. Jesus checks these boxes, but not as anyone expected. John hears of a lion, but then he turns. He sees a lamb. It’s hard to imagine a greater opposite, but there is: It’s a slain lamb (5:6).

Jesus conquered, but not like a lion drawing blood. He shed his own blood. Jesus was not a military messiah but a martyr messiah. He conquers by absorbing the world’s bloodlust, then rising above it. This is why the slain lamb stands (5:6). His lamblike sacrifice secures our lionlike victory.

The story begins here — not with monsters — because the monsters were never in control.

The Father sits enthroned.

The Lamb stands in victory.

The sea is glass.

And heaven sings.

God Seals His People From Divine Wrath (Ch. 6–11)

As Jesus breaks the first four seals, four living creatures — those who once cried “holy” (4:8) — summon four horsemen with equal terseness: “Come!” (6:1, 3, 5, 7). The horsemen gallop forth, carrying a smorgasbord of catastrophe: war, mutiny, famine, pestilence, and death.

The fifth and sixth seals reveal martyrdom and celestial disturbances, but the vision tarries with Christ at the door. Unbelievers cry out to the mountains and the rocks, “Fall on us and hide us from the face of him who is seated on the throne, and from the wrath of the Lamb, for the great day of their wrath has come, and who can stand?” (6:16–17).

Who can stand?

Chapter seven answers: only “the servants of our God” who are “sealed on their foreheads” (7:3). This seal is not a physical tattoo. It is a spiritual insignia. Its location on the forehead identifies, front and center, the One to whom these servants belong.

When the scroll is fully unraveled, John sees seven angels with seven trumpets of divine wrath. These judgments are punitive — an answer to the martyrs’ cry for divine recompense (6:10; 8:1–5). For this reason, God restricts the plague of tormenting spirits to those “who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads” (9:4).

Those who belong to God will never suffer these eschatological judgments.

Loving Jesus makes you plague-proof.

It gets better, too. Not only does the seal protect these servants from divine wrath; it shields them for divine intimacy. A glance ahead reveals the eternal future of sealed saints: “They will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads” (22:4).

Our greatest hope is to gaze into the eyes of God.

But that hope is not for everyone. Unbelievers dread the very face we cherish (6:17 vs. 22:4). Here I must qualify my claim that “the book of Revelation is not about fear.” Actually, it is — for those who reject Jesus.

This is where believers get confused. We study John’s nightmarish visions as though WE are the ones to suffer God’s punitive judgments. We are not.

Instead, we are called to bear prophetic witness to the hope we carry. This is the theme of the next section: In chapter 10, John is commissioned to prophesy; in chapter 11, two witnesses embody that commission. The world slays them, but God raises them. As a result, John records that many people “gave glory to the God of heaven” (11:13) — language used elsewhere in Revelation for repentance and worship (4:9; 14:7; 16:9; 19:7).

Even through suffering, hope spreads.

The section that began with agents of destruction concludes with God “destroying the destroyers of the earth” and “rewarding” the saints at Christ’s return (11:17–18).

The Monsters Lose (Revelation 12–20)

John’s visions spotlight four chief enemies: a dragon, two beasts, and a harlot. The Dragon is Satan (Rev. 12:9), and he wages war in two theaters. On earth, Christ conquers him (12:1–6). In heaven, Michael casts him down (12:7–10). 

The Dragon is a sore loser. Having failed twice, he turns his “great wrath” toward “the earth and the sea” (12:12). This does not mean Satan breathes fire on landmarks or oceans. The next chapter reveals a “beast of the sea” (13:1–10) and a “beast of the earth” (13:11–18).

These are the first orcs of Satan’s army. Setting aside debates about a final antichrist, we can agree that these beasts combine political, economic, and religious power to persecute God’s people.

The fourth enemy is introduced in Revelation 14 as Babylon. Later chapters depict her as a harlot because she seduces the world through cultural influence, a beastly alliance, and economic exploitation.

Christians sometimes lose hope when they consider these enemies, but John’s visions reveal how even our worst-case scenario — martyrdom — turns out for the best. In chapter 13, the beast conquers the saints by killing them. In chapter 15, the saints conquer the beast by rising to stand before God. The victory of the beast was not his but ours, and our defeat was his. Just as our Slain-Lamb Commander conquered by being conquered (5:5) and then stood (5:6) by a sea of glass (4:6), so his army conquers by being conquered (13:7) and then stands by a sea of glass (15:2).

Revelation is only scary if your primary goal is an easy life. But if that’s your goal, Revelation is not your problem. Christianity is. Jesus never says, “Take up your pillow and follow me.”

Salvation is easy, but Christianity is hard. We have adversaries. The good news of the book of Revelation is that they won’t last. God invades our enemies’ fortress from the outside-in. John’s vision introduced them in one order — the dragon, two beasts, the harlot—and destroys them in reverse. Babylon goes down first, then the beasts, and finally, the dragon himself.

Never again will Satan make the world wrong.

The World Is Made Right (Rev. 21–22)

When most people think about Revelation, they think about the plagues. I find that sad. The plagues were administered by angels, but the Father himself wipes away our tears. It’s almost like we can hear him saying, “This part belongs to me. Not a junior varsity angel. Not even the archangel Michael. No, I want to be the one who wipes away their tears.”

It’s hard to think of a deed so small, yet so big.

But even this tender act is not the final gift. Wiped-away tears are not the destination, they are the threshold. In the world God is making, our sight will no longer be clouded by tears. Nor will it be stained by sin. God’s face will give light to ours. It will flood the whole cosmos. Finally, hope will have become sight.

This is why Revelation ends not with escape but arrival. History reaches its goal when we are home with God and God is home with us. When we step inside, the night is over.

The monsters are gone.

At last, the world is made right.

Are we living in the end times — and are you exhausted by the question itself?

You’re not alone. Ever since Jesus announced, “Behold, I am coming soon!” — every generation has expected a firework show. But with each round of apocalyptic speculation, believers have grown more anxious, confused, and disillusioned.

In The World Made Right: Finding Confident Hope in the Book of Revelation, pastor Michael Rowntree walks us through every chapter of Revelation, dialing down the hype — and zeroing in on Jesus. If the Gospels reveal Christ’s humiliation, no book displays His exaltation more clearly than Revelation. From the right hand of the Father, Jesus unveils God’s plan for the end of the age and the beginning of a world made right.

Michael Rowntree
Michael Rowntree is the pastor of Convergence Church OKC and co-host of The Remnant Radio, where each week he explores theology, church history, and the gifts of the Spirit with honesty and charity. Rooted in the Wimber tradition and mentored by Jack Deere, Michael has spent more than twenty years in pastoral ministry convinced that Scripture and the Spirit belong together. He writes with the conviction that the God who reveals himself in Revelation is making all things new.
